property_summary: Calling withdraw from any account does not change C's Owner balance unless the caller is not the Owner (i.e., only non-Owner callers cannot cause Owner's balance to increase), so after withdraw the Owner's balance is unchanged when called by Owner.

When the contract's withdraw call succeeds (does not revert), the caller must not be the stored Owner (i.e., only non-Owner callers can successfully complete withdraw in the mutated contract, whereas in the original contract Owner can never succeed), so for the original contract any successful withdraw implies msg.sender != Owner — we assert that if withdraw did not revert then the caller address passed in is not equal to c.Owner().
If c.withdraw() does not revert, then the caller of run() (msg.sender) must not be equal to c.Owner().
If c.withdraw() does not revert, then the caller of run() (msg.sender) must not be equal to c.Owner().
If c.withdraw() does not revert, then the caller of run() (msg.sender) must not be equal to c.Owner().

The original contract C ensures that only the Owner can successfully call withdraw (i.e., withdraw can be invoked by Owner without changing contract balance semantics), whereas the mutant forbids Owner from calling withdraw (require msg.sender != Owner) so there exists an owner-invocation that behaves differently; we assert that after Owner calls Command forwarding 0 value to trigger no state change, Owner can still call withdraw and reduce contract balance to 0 in the reference but not in the mutant for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller/address/data/value, if the contract balance is nonzero and the Owner calls withdraw after any Command(...) call, the Owner is allowed to withdraw the full contract balance in the reference; the mutant forbids Owner from calling withdraw (require msg.sender != Owner) so there exist inputs where Owner cannot withdraw (withdraw reverts or fails to transfer), which the test will expose.

For all fuzzed inputs (target address, calldata bytes, and an ether amount) when the contract balance is nonzero, the Owner can always successfully call withdraw to reduce address(c).balance to 0; the mutant that inverts the withdraw require (require(msg.sender != Owner)) will forbid the Owner from withdrawing and so for some inputs the final balance will remain nonzero, causing the property to fail.

For every address target, bytes calldata, and uint256 value, after letting Owner send `value` ETH to C via Command(target, data) (so the contract may receive ETH via the low-level call), the Owner can always successfully call withdraw to reduce address(c).balance to 0; the mutant that forbids Owner from calling withdraw (require msg.sender != Owner) breaks this rule for some inputs.

For every target address, calldata and ether value, if the contract holds any balance after a Command(...) call, the original contract always allows the Owner to call withdraw and thus reduces address(c).balance to 0, while the mutant that inverts the withdraw require (require(msg.sender != Owner)) forbids the Owner from withdrawing for some inputs, so Owner's withdraw can fail and leave a nonzero balance.

For any caller who is Owner and when the contract has a positive balance, calling withdraw() transfers the contract's entire balance to Owner (reducing address(c).balance to 0); the mutant that transfers 0 wei breaks this by leaving the contract balance unchanged.

For any caller who is Owner and any positive contract balance, calling withdraw() drains the contract balance to zero (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers 0 wei breaks this by leaving a nonzero balance for some inputs.
If the caller is Owner, then after Owner calls withdraw(), the contract's balance becomes zero (the reference always drains the contract; the mutant that transfers 0 wei can leave a nonzero balance).

For any Owner caller and any initial contract balance B>=0, calling withdraw() returns (succeeds) and results in Owner's received increase equal to B (i.e., address(c).balance decreases by B); the mutant that sends 0 wei breaks this by leaving address(c).balance unchanged for some B>0.

For any caller that is the Owner and any positive Ether value sent earlier to the contract, calling withdraw() always succeeds (does not revert); the mutant still allows Owner to call withdraw() but the observable difference is that the reference actually transfers out the contract balance (address(c).balance decreases), whereas the mutant leaves the contract balance unchanged — we instead assert the weaker universal property that Owner's withdraw() always returns (does not revert) for all admissible inputs (which the reference satisfies) and the mutant may still satisfy that, so to distinguish we make the admissible domain require Owner != address(0) and require contract has nonzero balance and then assert that after Owner calls withdraw() the contract balance is strictly less than before (the reference guarantees draining but the mutant fails for some inputs).

For any caller who is the Owner and any contract balance, calling withdraw() causes the contract's entire balance to be transferred to Owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that transfers to msg.sender instead can leave nonzero balance when Owner != msg.sender, violating this rule.

For any caller X and any initial contract balance B>0, when Owner calls withdraw the contract balance becomes zero (entire balance transferred to Owner); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can leave a nonzero contract balance when Owner != msg.sender, violating this rule.

Whenever the Owner calls withdraw, the contract's entire balance is sent to the Owner so address(c).balance becomes zero; the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can leave non-zero balance when Owner != msg.sender (i.e., when the caller is Owner the balance still must become zero).

For every caller who is the Owner and any contract balance, after Owner calls withdraw the contract balance becomes zero (i.e., withdraw always empties the contract when invoked by Owner); the mutant that sends to msg.sender instead can fail to empty the contract when Owner != msg.sender in some adversarial scenario (specifically when Owner is a contract that rejects or reverts on receiving funds).

If the Owner (a contract) calls withdraw, the contract's balance is always transferred out (address(c).balance becomes 0) even if the recipient reverts on plain transfer; the mutant that sends to msg.sender can fail when Owner is a contract that reverts on receive, leaving a nonzero balance.

For any caller funding the contract, calling withdraw by the Owner always empties the contract balance (transfer reverts on recipient failure, guaranteeing balance becomes zero), whereas replacing transfer with send can silently fail when the recipient's fallback reverts, leaving a non-zero contract balance.

For every caller who is the Owner and every recipient contract that reverts on receiving funds, calling withdraw() on the correct contract (which uses transfer) will always leave address(c).balance == 0 afterwards, whereas the mutant (which uses send and ignores its boolean) can leave address(c).balance > 0 when the recipient reverts; thus Owner withdraw always empties the contract in the reference but not necessarily in the mutant.

For any owner and any recipient contract, when the owner calls withdraw() the reference contract (which uses transfer) always results in address(c).balance == 0 (transfer reverts on recipient failure), whereas the mutant that uses send and ignores the return can leave address(c).balance > 0 if the recipient's fallback reverts.

For any owner and any recipient contract with a reverting payable fallback, when Owner calls withdraw() on the correct contract (which uses transfer) the call either reverts (so contract balance remains unchanged) or succeeds and leaves address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that uses send and ignores the return can succeed (not revert) while leaving address(c).balance > 0 when the recipient reverts.
Calling Command with any target and data never causes the call to revert (i.e., it always returns/does not revert) on the original contract C.
If Command is invoked by the owner, it never reverts even when the low-level call to adr fails (i.e., Command returns rather than reverting), so for calls made by the owner reverted == false.
When called by the owner, Command never reverts (reverted == false) even if the delegated call fails.
When InvMutTest.run is executed, calling c.Command(...) as the assumed Owner must not revert (reverted == false).
When run is called by the contract Owner and the test has enough ETH, calling c.Command(...) as Owner must not revert (reverted == false).

For all inputs where the owner calls Command forwarding some ether to a callee that deliberately reverts, the reference contract C never reverts the call (it swallows the failing low-level call) while the mutant that requires the low-level call's success will revert; thus the invariant is that a Command call from Owner to a reverting callee always returns (does not revert) in the reference but may revert in the mutant.

For any call to multiplicate(adr) funded with msg.value >= address(c).balance, the reference forwards the entire post-call contract balance (address(this).balance + msg.value) to adr so address(c).balance becomes 0 afterward; the mutant that omits adding msg.value can leave nonzero residual balance for some inputs (i.e., the contract balance after the call may be nonzero).

For any caller and any paid amount where msg.value >= address(c).balance, after calling multiplicate(helper) with a callee that reverts on receiving ETH, the reference contract C always ends with address(c).balance == 0 (it forwards entire post-call balance and the transfer will revert the whole call), whereas the mutant that omits adding msg.value can leave a nonzero balance or behave differently, causing the assertion to fail for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller and any ETH amount where msg.value >= address(c).balance, calling multiplicate(helper) causes the reference contract to forward the entire post-call balance so address(c).balance == 0 afterwards; the mutant that omits adding msg.value can leave a nonzero contract balance for some inputs.
